chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah ibn Mihran said:

I asked him about a man who ate or drank after the dawn had risen in the month of Ramadan, so he said: 'If he got up, looked, and did not see the dawn, then ate, and then returned and saw the dawn, let him complete his fast and there is no re-performance (qada') upon him. And if he got up, ate or drank, and then looked at the dawn and saw that it had risen, let him complete his fast and perform a re-performance (qada') for another day, because he began with eating before looking, so re-performance is upon him.' And this does not contradict what was narrated:

key_terms.اَلْفَجْرُ: Dawn (the time for Fajr prayer begins)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on breaking the fast due to eating after dawn if one did not check for sunrise first?
ai.summary: This narration from Sahih al-Tusi clarifies the distinction between unintentional error (ghalat) and negligence in determining the onset of Fajr, a key topic in Usul al-Fiqh regarding the validity of acts of worship. It establishes that mere failure to check does not invalidate the fast, but eating before verifying the time implies a lack of due diligence, necessitating a make-up day (qada') in addition to completing the current fast. This ruling reflects the Shia emphasis on the obligation of seeking knowledge of the prayer and fasting times as a prerequisite for valid worship.
